source_text: Τίς ἂν οὖν ἀνάστασιν πεπιστευκὼς ἐπὶ σώμασιν ἀναστησομένοις ἑαυτὸν παράσχοι τάφον; Οὐ γὰρ τῶν αὐτῶν καὶ ἀναστήσεσθαι ἡμῶν πεπεῖσθαι τὰ σώματα καὶ ἐσθίειν αὐτὰ ὡς οὐκ ἀναστησόμενα, καὶ ἀποδώσειν μὲν νομίζειν τὴν γῆν τοὺς ἰδίους νεκρούς, οὓς δέ τις αὐτὸς ἐγκατέθαψεν αὐτῷ μήτε ἀπαιτηθήσεσθαι. Τοὐναντίον μὲν οὖν εἰκὸς τοὺς μὲν μήτε λόγον ὑφέξειν τοῦ ἐνταῦθα ἢ πονηροῦ ἢ χρηστοῦ βίου μήτε ἀνάστασιν εἶναι οἰομένους, συναπόλλυσθαι δὲ τῷ σώματι καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ οἷον ἐναποσβέννυσθαι λογιζομένους, μηδενὸς ἂν ἀποσχέσθαι τολμήματος· τοὺς δὲ μηδὲν ἀνεξέταστον ἔσεσθαι παρὰ τῷ θεῷ, συγκολασθήσεσθαι δὲ καὶ τὸ ὑπουργῆσαν σῶμα ταῖς ἀλόγοις ὁρμαῖς τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ ἐπιθυμίαις πεπεισμένους, οὐδεὶς λόγος ἔχει οὐδὲ τῶν βραχυτάτων τι ἁμαρτεῖν. Εἰ δέ τῳ λῆρος πολὺς δοκεῖ, τὸ σαπὲν καὶ διαλυθὲν καὶ ἀφανισθὲν σῶμα συστῆναι πάλιν, κακίας μὲν οὐκ ἂν εἰκότως δόξαν ἀποφεροίμεθα διὰ τοὺς οὐ πιστεύοντας ἀλλ᾿ εὐηθείας· οἷς γὰρ ἀπατῶμεν ἑαυτοὺς λόγοις ἀδικοῦμεν οὐδένα. Ὅτι μέντοι οὐ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς μόνον ἀναστήσεται τὰ σώματα, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ πολλοὺς τῶν φιλοσόφων, περίεργον ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος δεικνύειν, ἵνα μὴ ἐξαγωνίους τοῖς προκειμένοις ἐπεισάγειν δοκῶμεν λόγους, ἢ περὶ νοητῶν καὶ αἰσθητῶν καὶ τῆς τούτων συστάσεως λέγοντες, ἢ ὅτι πρεσβύτερα τὰ ἀσώματα τῶν σωμάτων καὶ τὰ νοητὰ προάγει τῶν αἰσθητῶν, κἂν πρώτοις περιπίπτωμεν τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς, συνισταμένων ἐκ μὲν τῶν ἀσωμάτων κατὰ τὴν ἐπισύνθεσιν τῶν νοητῶν σωμάτων, ἐκ δὲ τῶν νοητῶν τῶν αἰσθητῶν· οὐ γὰρ κωλύει κατὰ τὸν Πυθαγόραν καὶ τὸν Πλάτωνα, γενομένης τῆς διαλύσεως τῶν σωμάτων, ἐξ ὧν τὴν ἀρχὴν συνέστη ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν αὐτὰ καὶ πάλιν συστῆναι. Ἀλλ᾿ ἀνακείσθω μὲν ὁ περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγος.
pass_a_gloss: Who then having believed in resurrection concerning bodies to be resurrected would provide a grave for himself? For it is not of the same things to be persuaded that our bodies will also rise and to eat them as if they will not rise, and to think that the earth will give back its own dead, which someone himself has buried for himself, will not be demanded back. On the contrary, it is likely that those who do not expect an account of the life here, either bad or good, and do not think there is a resurrection, will perish together with the body and the soul, and will be extinguished, as it were, and will not abstain from any daring act; but for those who have nothing unexamined before God, their body, which has served the irrational impulses and desires of the soul, will be punished together, and no one will have an excuse, nor will they commit even the smallest sin. But if to someone it seems a lot of nonsense, that the rotten and dissolved and vanished body will be restored again, we would not reasonably be accused of wickedness, but of simplicity, because we deceive no one with our words, for we wrong no one. That, however, the bodies will rise not only according to us, but also according to many philosophers, it is superfluous to show at present, lest we seem to introduce extraneous arguments, either when speaking about intelligible and sensible things and their composition, or that the bodiless things are older than bodies and the intelligible things precede the sensible things, and even if we first encounter the sensible things, they are composed of the bodiless things according to the synthesis of the intelligible bodies, and of the intelligible things, the sensible things; for it does not prevent, according to Pythagoras and Plato, that after the dissolution of the bodies, from which they were originally composed, they can be composed again from the same things. But let the discussion about the resurrection be set aside.

pass_b_english: Who, having believed in a resurrection of bodies, would provide a grave for himself? It is inconsistent to be persuaded that our bodies will rise and yet treat them as if they will not—eating them, thinking the earth will return its own dead, which someone buried for himself, without demanding them back. On the contrary, those who expect no account of the life here, whether bad or good, and who do not think there is a resurrection, will likely perish together with body and soul, being as it were extinguished, and will abstain from no daring act. But for those convinced that nothing will go unexamined before God, and that the body which served the soul's irrational impulses and desires will be punished together with it, no one has any excuse, nor will they commit even the smallest sin. If the restoration of a rotten, dissolved, and vanished body seems like sheer nonsense to someone, we would not reasonably be accused of wickedness, but of simplicity, since we deceive no one with our words, for we wrong no one. That bodies will rise not only according to us but also according to many philosophers is superfluous to demonstrate at present, lest we seem to introduce extraneous arguments—whether when speaking about intelligible and sensible things and their composition, or that bodiless things are older than bodies and intelligible things precede sensible ones, and even if we first encounter sensible things, they are composed of bodiless things according to the synthesis of intelligible bodies, and sensible things from intelligible ones; for according to Pythagoras and Plato, after the dissolution of bodies, the elements from which they were originally composed can be composed again from the same things. But let the discussion about the resurrection be set aside.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional and causal structures of the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Greek. The philosophical references to Pythagoras and Plato are correctly rendered. The distinction between 'wickedness' (κακίας) and 'simplicity/goodwill' (εὐηθείας) is preserved.
